title: The Ship That Would Not Settle
paragraphs: According to Plutarch, the Athenians preserved the ship on which Theseus had returned from Crete, replacing its timbers one by one as they decayed. Plutarch adds that philosophers used the ship as an example in debates about things that grow: some held that it remained the same ship, others that it did not. The puzzle has long outlived the timber.

Thomas Hobbes later added a twist that makes the problem far less comfortable. Suppose someone collected the discarded planks and reassembled them in their original order. Now there are two ships, each with a respectable claim: one has continuity of form and use, the other has every original piece. Whichever we choose, we seem to surrender an intuition we thought we held firmly.

Philosophers have proposed several exits. Some say identity over time is a matter of continuity, so the repaired ship wins. Others treat the question as partly verbal: 'same ship' has more than one legitimate meaning, and the puzzle merely forces us to notice which one we were using. A more radical view holds that an object is not wholly present at any moment but is spread out across time, much like an event.

Each answer purchases tidiness at a price. The continuity view must explain why the reassembled original feels like a serious rival rather than a pile of recycled wood. The verbal view risks implying that nothing deep was ever at stake, which seems too quick: insurance claims, museum labels and court rulings about ownership depend on settling which object is which.

Perhaps the ship's real lesson concerns us rather than the vessel. Many of our cells are replaced over the years, our memories can shift as we recall them, and yet we rarely doubt that we are the same person who began reading this paragraph. That confidence may be justified, but it is not obviously better grounded than the Athenians' confidence in their ship.
